canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Test the most likely artifact before changing the chain: Trim the input down, recreate the previous loudness after the processor, and compare whether the effect becomes more stable.
stopOrUndo: Stop once you can reliably judge transient shape, low-end stability, and whether occasional peaks stop producing abrupt grit. Back off or undo immediately if lower input can remove the intended color; excessive input can turn a bus tone move into uncontrolled clipping.
Bypass the processor and restore the saved input, output, mix, timing, and routing values; if a duplicate or parallel path was created, mute or remove it.
canonicalCards.teachingPrinciple: Headroom is not a magic target, but the level entering a nonlinear processor defines its operating point and whether peaks receive subtle color or hard flattening.

canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Build a clean listening reference: Drive a bus gently, level-match, and compare at quiet monitoring level and in mono.
stopOrUndo: Stop once you can reliably judge center stability, low-mid density, transient openness, and front-to-back depth. Back off or undo immediately if small apparent glue can be only level or high-frequency loss, while excess drive can collapse contrast.
Bypass the processor and restore the saved input, output, mix, timing, and routing values; if a duplicate or parallel path was created, mute or remove it.
canonicalCards.teachingPrinciple: Console and transformer labels can include nonlinear core behavior, frequency response, crosstalk, and gain staging; the useful test is whether hierarchy and depth survive.
canonicalCards.title: Transformer and console-style saturation — what it changes
tradeoffs: Small apparent glue can be only level or high-frequency loss, while excess drive can collapse contrast.
A louder or peak-reduced version can seem better before the actual timbral or envelope change is judged.
A local improvement can create a new masking, headroom, phase, noise, or arrangement problem.
canonicalCards.userIntent: Concept and listening foundation for add subtle cohesion and tone.

canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Test the most likely artifact before changing the chain: Increase attack until the onset becomes obvious, then back off while listening in the full mix.
stopOrUndo: Stop once you can reliably judge definition, front-to-back position, click/pick noise, and whether body still connects. Back off or undo immediately if too much attack can sound detached, small, or brittle and can consume peak headroom.
Bypass the processor and restore the saved input, output, mix, timing, and routing values; if a duplicate or parallel path was created, mute or remove it.

myths.correction: Saturation is a form of nonlinear distortion; the useful distinction is amount, curve, dynamics, and audible intent.
myths.myth: Saturation is not distortion

myths.correction: Real processors create level- and frequency-dependent mixtures; intermodulation, filtering, and source context matter more than a slogan.
myths.myth: Even harmonics are always warm and odd harmonics are always harsh

myths.correction: A label is a model hypothesis, not proof of circuit equivalence or artistic superiority.
myths.myth: Analog-mode labels guarantee analog sound

myths.correction: More drive can flatten transients, generate harshness, raise noise, and reduce depth.
myths.myth: More drive always means more warmth

myths.correction: Nonlinear processing can distort far below digital full scale depending on its operating point.
myths.myth: If the meter is not clipping, distortion cannot be happening

myths.correction: Clipping is static nonlinear waveform reshaping; limiting is time-varying gain control, even if both reduce peaks.
myths.myth: A clipper is just a limiter with zero attack

myths.correction: Soft clipping can still create audible harmonics, intermodulation, aliasing, and transient loss.
myths.myth: Soft clipping is always transparent

myths.correction: Shallow, controlled hard clipping can be useful on brief peaks or as a deliberate effect; amount and source decide.
myths.myth: Hard clipping is always unusable

myths.correction: Oversampling trades aliasing reduction against filters, CPU, latency, and possible tone changes.
myths.myth: Maximum oversampling is always best

myths.correction: Oversampling targets aliasing; it does not remove intermodulation, harsh transfer curves, noise, or poor gain staging.
myths.myth: Oversampling removes all distortion artifacts

myths.correction: Aliasing produces folded, often inharmonic components; ordinary harmonics remain integer-related before folding.
myths.myth: Aliasing is the same as harmonic distortion

myths.correction: It may increase density or soften peaks, but cohesion is a listening judgment affected by balance and arrangement.
myths.myth: Saturation automatically glues a mix

myths.correction: It can round peaks and raise density, but it lacks the same controllable detector, ratio, attack, and release behavior.
myths.myth: Saturation can replace compression in every case

myths.correction: Order changes both detector behavior and harmonic generation; neither order is universal.
myths.myth: Compression must always come before saturation

myths.correction: Pre- and post-EQ solve different problems; compare based on what should drive the nonlinear stage.
myths.myth: EQ must always come before saturation

myths.correction: Latency, filtering, nonlinear phase, and blend can create combing or low-end changes.
myths.myth: Parallel saturation cannot change phase or tone if the dry signal remains

myths.correction: Crossovers and multiple detectors can add complexity and artifacts; targeted does not mean transparent.
myths.myth: Multiband saturation is automatically cleaner

myths.correction: Upper harmonics can help, but full-band low-end distortion can reduce headroom and create intermodulation.
myths.myth: Saturating the sub always improves translation

myths.correction: Tape machines and emulations differ in speed, bias, head, electronics, noise, modulation, and calibration.
myths.myth: Tape saturation is one identifiable sound

myths.correction: Tube circuits and models vary with topology, bias, feedback, level, filtering, and source.
myths.myth: Tube saturation means mostly even harmonics

myths.correction: A model or device can range from nearly clean to strongly nonlinear depending on level and design.
myths.myth: Transformer saturation is automatically subtle

myths.correction: Exciters generate harmonics and can affect sibilance, noise, and perceived harshness as well as brightness.
myths.myth: Exciters only add air

myths.correction: Bit-depth reduction and rate reduction create different quantization and imaging artifacts.
myths.myth: Bitcrushing and sample-rate reduction are the same effect

myths.correction: It can add readable harmonics, but translation still depends on balance, notes, arrangement, and playback.
myths.myth: Saturation always makes bass louder on small speakers

myths.correction: Loudness bias must be removed before judging tone or density.
myths.myth: A louder saturated version proves the processor helped

myths.correction: It can color a performance but cannot reliably create missing timing, phrasing, emotion, or arrangement contrast.
myths.myth: Saturation fixes a boring performance

myths.correction: Broadened spectra and added sustain can increase masking even when solo tone is flattering.
myths.myth: If saturation sounds good solo, it will help the mix

myths.correction: A spectrum can show energy changes, not the subjective meaning or musical value of warmth.
myths.myth: A spectrum analyzer can prove that saturation sounds warm

myths.correction: Transient processors often respond to envelope change rather than the same absolute-level threshold model.
myths.myth: Transient shaping is just compression without a threshold

myths.correction: On a transient shaper, attack often means boosting or cutting the onset, not delaying gain reduction.
myths.myth: Attack control always means compressor attack time

myths.correction: It changes existing later-envelope energy; it does not synthesize a new acoustic space.
myths.myth: Sustain control creates reverb

myths.correction: It can create click, brittleness, high peaks, or separation from the body.
myths.myth: Boosting attack always makes drums punchier

myths.correction: Too much reduction can make timing vague, late, or lifeless.
myths.myth: Reducing attack always moves a source back naturally

myths.correction: It can also raise bleed, noise, room, and overlap that makes the arrangement smaller.
myths.myth: Increasing sustain always makes a sound bigger

myths.correction: Transient sustain reduction and gates use different detection and envelope behavior.
myths.myth: Reducing sustain is the same as gating

myths.correction: Global shaping applies a rule; irregular events may need clip gain, editing, or re-recording.
myths.myth: A transient shaper can fix any inconsistent performance

myths.correction: Attack and sustain changes alter peak and average level and require fair output compensation.
myths.myth: Transient shaping does not affect level

myths.correction: It can introduce filtering, phase, detector, or separation artifacts and encourages over-targeting.
myths.myth: Frequency-selective transient processing is always safer

myths.correction: Crossover and band recombination behavior still matter.
myths.myth: Multiband transient shaping has no crossover tradeoff

myths.correction: Latency and phase can change the combined tone, and added attacks can create new peaks.
myths.myth: Parallel transient shaping preserves the dry sound perfectly

myths.correction: Order depends on whether the compressor should respond to the reshaped envelope.
myths.myth: Transient shaping before compression is always correct

myths.correction: It may emphasize compression artifacts, noise, or a click without restoring the original dynamics.
myths.myth: Transient shaping after compression always restores lost punch

myths.correction: Overheads often carry the whole kit image, room, snare, and stereo timing.
myths.myth: Overheads are safe to transient-shape because they are mostly cymbals

myths.correction: Plosives are event- and frequency-specific; manual or targeted editing is usually safer.
myths.myth: A transient shaper can remove plosives cleanly across a vocal

myths.correction: Bass impact also depends on note timing, body, sub envelope, harmonics, and kick relationship.
myths.myth: Bass punch is only about attack

myths.correction: Registers, dynamics, pedal, and phrase context respond differently.
myths.myth: Piano attack can be fixed globally without affecting musicality

myths.correction: Audible envelope or spectral changes may be subtle; conversely, visible changes do not prove improvement.
myths.myth: If there is no visible waveform change, transient shaping did nothing

myths.correction: Detector response depends on level, timing, bleed, and source envelope.
myths.myth: The same transient setting works on every hit

myths.correction: Severe correction can create artifacts and consume more time than a better source.
myths.myth: Extreme transient shaping is faster than re-recording

myths.correction: It is a processor the user must insert and adjust; TrackSmith Tutor has no execution authority.
myths.myth: Logic Enveloper can automatically change Logic for the user
